title: In-place conversion of ordinary ground into a specified engineering solid

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to turn a selected volume of natural ground, while leaving it in place, into an engineering material with strength, stiffness, and permeability specified in advance. Its intended scope is a heterogeneous ground mass comparable to a city block or dam foundation, with sufficiently predictable properties throughout that volume to support engineering design. Success would require durable performance and an affordable treatment process, rather than simply stronger individual soil specimens. This is the target capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Conventional deep mixing and grouting already improve soil engineering properties. Microbially induced carbonate precipitation, or MICP, offers another relevant mechanism: biological activity promotes calcite formation within pore spaces, binding soil particles together. The distinctive ambition here is dependable control of an entire selected ground volume across natural variability. The supplied evidence identifies obstacles to that ambition for MICP, but does not establish the limits of every conventional or emerging treatment method.

significance.text: As a conditional engineering judgment, achieving this capability would make existing ground a more predictable design material. In suitable settings, engineers could design foundations around specified treated-ground properties and reduce excavation, replacement, or reliance on foundations that transfer loads through weak layers. The revolutionary aspect would be reliable control over a heterogeneous volume at useful scale and cost, rather than the already demonstrated ability to strengthen soil locally.

Liquefaction mitigation is a technically grounded potential application. The December 2024 MICP review describes particle cementation and reports improved resistance to re-liquefaction in treated specimens. Those findings support investigating mitigation, but do not demonstrate elimination of liquefaction susceptibility throughout an occupied district. Such an application would require verified cyclic performance, adequate treatment coverage, and control of treatment effects on existing structures and groundwater, as well as practical access beneath buildings and infrastructure.

Stabilizing thawing permafrost remains a separate possible application. The review discusses wet–dry and freeze–thaw durability testing, but resistance to those cycles does not by itself establish prevention of thaw settlement or stabilization of ice-rich ground. Likewise, adequate treated-ground properties would not alone establish that buildings remain immediately occupiable after an earthquake; ground response, foundations, and structural performance must also be assessed.

The analogy to manufacturing a specified solid has practical limits. Treated foundation soil need not attain concrete-like compressive strength to be useful, and strength alone does not determine foundation suitability. The intended advance is control of the combination of properties required by a particular site and loading condition. Reduced excavation, district-scale seismic mitigation, and permafrost stabilization are conditional consequences, not established outcomes of the reported specimen results.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in the supplied research is uniform, durable, and affordable treatment of varied natural soils at large field scale to meet properties chosen before treatment. For MICP in low-cohesive soils, the December 2024 review specifically identifies uniform calcite precipitation across heterogeneous ground, field durability, and project-scale economics as continuing challenges. The record does not justify ranking MICP as the leading biological route or declaring that every other technology fails across the entire proposed scope.

Engineering synthesis: closing the gap requires connecting a treatment process to predictable spatial distributions of strength, stiffness, and permeability. A satisfactory average result would be insufficient if untreated pockets or weak regions controlled foundation behavior. Engineers would need a defensible way to account for natural variability, verify treatment throughout the selected volume, and translate measured properties and their uncertainty into a usable ground model.

Durability must also be established under operational loads and relevant environmental conditions. The review calls for pilot projects under working geostructures and natural climatic stresses, together with long-term field monitoring. Laboratory aging can help identify degradation mechanisms, but it does not establish service-life performance for a particular field installation. Project-scale affordability remains an additional barrier even if the material response is technically satisfactory.

current_state.text: Liu, Beng, Wu, and coauthors published their review, “Microbial induced calcite precipitation for improving low-cohesive soil: mechanisms, methods and macroscopic properties,” on 29 December 2024. It documents an in-situ particle-binding mechanism and experimental improvements in soil properties, while identifying uniform precipitation and project-scale cost as barriers. This is a dated synthesis of MICP research, not a demonstration of the full city-block or dam-foundation capability proposed here.

The review reports that strengthening gains exceeding 2 MPa are commonly achieved at calcium carbonate contents of approximately 8–14%. This describes reported gains, not an upper bound on treated-soil strength. It also reports peak strengths of 14 MPa for sand specimens produced by ex-situ mixing at 24% carbonate content. These results concern different treatment conditions and carbonate contents; the 14 MPa specimen result neither contradicts the lower-content statement nor demonstrates conversion of an in-place ground mass.

For material context, Heveran and Hernandez’s “Make engineered living materials carry their weight,” published on 1 November 2023, lists a representative concrete compressive-strength range of 20–30 MPa. The supplied source is its accepted manuscript in the NSF Public Access Repository. That range is neither universal for concrete nor an acceptance threshold for treated foundation soil. Comparing it directly with a reported strengthening gain would also conflate an increase in strength with a final material strength.

The 2024 review also reports improved resilience against re-liquefaction in bio-grouted specimens and discusses wet–dry and freeze–thaw aging protocols. These are relevant partial achievements and evaluation methods. They do not establish safe treatment beneath occupied districts, long-term performance of a large heterogeneous ground mass, or stabilization of thawing permafrost.

The supplied evidence review assessed the MICP article through retained HTML prose that omitted figure images and expanded table contents. Its numerical assessment therefore supports what the article reports in prose, rather than an independent reading of Figure 9 or reanalysis of the underlying experiments. Although the source index also lists a saved PDF, the supplied review does not establish that it was used to resolve those omissions. For the Heveran and Hernandez manuscript, the review had complete 20-page text and checked the concrete table’s column headings; figure images were not inspected and were unnecessary for that table entry.

The supplied record contains no completed freshness search establishing developments through November 2026. Consequently, it supports the dated findings above but leaves unresolved whether the general target capability remains unavailable across all technologies at that date. The absence of an updated demonstration in this record is not evidence that none exists elsewhere.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: treat a heterogeneous natural-soil block at least tens of metres in plan and several metres thick, leaving it in place under a realistic water table. Before treatment, specify numerical acceptance limits for strength, stiffness, permeability, and allowable spatial variation, together with the intended foundation loads and ground conditions. These dimensions and conditions are proposed evaluation criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: In-place treatment of tens-of-metres ground blocks with prespecified acceptance limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed verification: define sampling coverage and measurement methods in advance, with enough spatial resolution to assess weak regions and treatment boundaries as well as average properties. Demonstrate that the resulting ground supports the intended engineering design. For a liquefaction-mitigation claim, include relevant cyclic loading and assessment of residual susceptibility. For treatment beneath occupied structures, separately demonstrate access, coverage, and acceptable effects on structures and groundwater.
completion_criteria.label: Spatially resolved verification demonstrates treated ground supports intended engineering design

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability demonstration: monitor the treated volume for a period measured in years under realistic loading and site-relevant exposure, including wet–dry or freeze–thaw cycles where applicable. Define allowable property loss and deformation before the trial. This proposal follows the review’s rationale for operational pilot projects and long-term monitoring, but the particular duration and acceptance thresholds remain to be chosen. A finite monitoring period would establish observed durability over that period, not lifetime performance.
completion_criteria.label: Years of field monitoring demonstrate durability within predefined performance limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed economic and reproducibility requirements: report treatment, verification, monitoring, and any necessary maintenance costs against excavation-and-replacement or deep foundations serving the same site requirements. Set an affordability threshold beforehand; merely reporting a cost does not demonstrate affordability. Repeat the demonstration across independent sites and treatment executions spanning explicitly described soils and groundwater conditions. Laboratory coupons alone would not meet this field scope, and even successful multi-site trials would establish demonstrated breadth rather than literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independent-site demonstrations meet preset affordability thresholds using full cost comparisons

related_concepts.text: Roster-based interpretation: CIV-02, “Mechanics-based prediction of earthquake liquefaction and its ground consequences,” addresses prediction, whereas CIV-03 addresses physical modification of ground. Predictive mechanics could help select treatment targets and assess residual ground consequences, but treatment does not itself supply that prediction. CIV-09, “Immediate building occupancy after the design earthquake, at life-safety cost,” addresses a broader building-performance outcome to which ground improvement might contribute. Neither concept is fulfilled merely by meeting CIV-03’s treated-ground property targets. These distinctions follow from the supplied titles; their complete specifications were not provided.

Roster-based interpretation: CIV-07, “Load-bearing engineered living materials for ordinary structures,” overlaps with CIV-03 when biological processes create load-bearing material. Their targets differ: CIV-03 concerns conversion of existing heterogeneous ground, while CIV-07 concerns engineered living materials for structures. Use of microbial activity to precipitate a binder does not by itself establish that the finished treated soil remains a living material or satisfies CIV-07. CIV-01, “A primary structural binder at global cement scale without process carbon dioxide,” concerns binder production, emissions, and global scale; CIV-03 does not establish those outcomes.

Roster-based interpretation: CIV-06, “Underground routes and spaces at surface-infrastructure cost,” could potentially benefit from controllable ground properties, but low-cost underground construction requires capabilities beyond soil treatment. CIV-04’s repeated recovery after cracking, CIV-05’s tensile-ductile mineral structures, CIV-10’s energy-storing concrete, CIV-11’s corrosion-free reinforcement, and CIV-12’s adaptive structural response concern separate material or structural functions. CIV-08 concerns reservoir sediment passage and carryover storage. None of those functions follows from the ground-conversion capability proposed here.

The research describes CIV-03 as the mitigation half of a historical liquefaction bundle. That is a useful organizing interpretation alongside CIV-02’s prediction focus, but the historical bundle itself was not supplied and its exact coverage cannot be verified. The entries therefore remain distinct, and the suggested permafrost application remains conditional rather than an established extension of scope.

change_log.change: Preserved CIV-03’s ID, title, and target of large-volume, in-place ground conversion to specified engineering properties.
change_log.reason: The concept remains meaningful despite uncertainty about individual supporting claims and present-day technological availability.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical limits on deep mixing and grouting with a narrower statement about what the supplied evidence establishes; removed the unsupported ranking of MICP as the leading biological route.
change_log.reason: The review supports established conventional improvement and dated MICP barriers, but not a comprehensive comparison across technologies.

change_log.change: Retained the reported gains above 2 MPa at 8–14% carbonate and integrated the omitted 14 MPa ex-situ specimen result at 24% carbonate.
change_log.reason: The earlier comparison could be read as imposing a strength ceiling that the supplied review does not support.

change_log.change: Reframed the 20–30 MPa concrete range as representative context and distinguished final strength from strengthening gain.
change_log.reason: The concrete table does not establish a universal range, a MICP ceiling, or the strength necessary for foundation suitability.

change_log.change: Preserved reduced excavation and liquefaction mitigation as conditional benefits while qualifying occupied-district deployment and thawing-permafrost stabilization.
change_log.reason: Specimen cementation, cyclic response, and freeze–thaw testing do not establish those broader field applications.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria to include predefined numerical limits, spatial verification, affordability, reproducibility, and explicit application boundaries.
change_log.reason: The original proposed trial dimensions and cost reporting alone would not establish predictable, affordable treatment or generality.

change_log.change: Preserved the source-review access limitations and separated dated findings from unverified November 2026 field status.
change_log.reason: Saved artifacts and retrieval dates do not establish that omitted figures were assessed or that a current technology survey was completed.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster to explain title-level overlaps while retaining uncertainty about full concept boundaries and the historical liquefaction bundle.
change_log.reason: The roster permits useful distinctions beyond those available to the earlier reviewer, but does not supply complete specifications.

unresolved_issues: Whether any technology has demonstrated the full target capability by November 2026 remains unresolved because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The comparative capabilities, costs, and limits of conventional deep mixing, grouting, MICP, and other approaches across the proposed scope are not established.
The reported MICP strength figures were assessed from review prose, without independent inspection of Figure 9 or reanalysis of the underlying studies.
Site-specific acceptance limits, sampling coverage, exposure conditions, monitoring duration, and an affordability threshold remain to be defined for a convincing demonstration.
Safe deployment beneath occupied districts and effective stabilization of thawing permafrost require application-specific evidence.
Complete specifications for related roster entries and the historical liquefaction bundle were not supplied; relationships beyond title-level distinctions remain provisional.

brief.title: Ground made to order without digging it up
possible: Engineers could turn the ground beneath a building or dam into a material with properties chosen in advance, while leaving it in place. They could specify its strength, stiffness—how much it deforms under load—and permeability—how easily water passes through it—throughout the treated volume.
why: Predictable ground would give engineers more options for foundations. In suitable places, they could reduce excavation and soil replacement, or reduce reliance on deep foundations that carry loads past weak ground.

sources.who: Zhengwei Liu, Jianping Beng, Yun Wu and colleagues
sources.showed: Their review describes how bacteria help form calcite, a mineral that binds soil grains. Experiments report stronger treated soil and better resistance to repeated liquefaction, when shaking makes ground lose strength.
sources.quote:
In the case of specialized 
rock materials like sandstone, the self-adsorption biphase 
injection method has been shown to regulate the uniform 
distribution of microorganisms effectively.
sources.cited_for: Bacterial treatment can improve soil properties, while uniform treatment, lasting performance and cost remain challenges.
sources.not_established: The reviewed experiments do not establish predictable, durable and affordable treatment throughout a large volume of varied natural ground.

sources.who: Chelsea M. Heveran and Christopher J. Hernandez
sources.showed: Their perspective compares the strength and stiffness of engineered living materials, which contain living organisms, with those of construction materials, including concrete.
sources.quote: The most rigid of ELMs reported so far employ microbial biomineralization.
sources.cited_for: Comparisons with construction materials put reported soil strengths in context.
sources.not_established: Concrete strength is not an acceptance threshold for treated ground, and material comparisons do not demonstrate treatment in place.

shown: Liu and colleagues describe stronger soil specimens and improved resistance to repeated liquefaction after bacterial treatment. Some strong sand specimens were made by mixing outside the ground. Neither result establishes control throughout a natural ground mass comparable to a city block.
missing: Treatment must reliably meet chosen properties throughout varied natural ground, including its weakest pockets.
Large treated volumes need demonstrated durability under working loads and environmental stresses.
Independent field trials need to meet preset affordability limits after verification, monitoring and maintenance costs are included.

milestones.label: A large ground block meets properties chosen beforehand
milestones.explanation: A trial would have to treat varied ground tens of metres across and metres deep under a realistic water table, meeting preset property and variation limits. This would test control at a useful foundation scale.

milestones.label: Measurements show the ground supports its intended design
milestones.explanation: Measurements planned beforehand would have to assess weak spots and boundaries and establish suitability for the intended design. Shaking resistance and work beneath occupied buildings would need specific checks.

milestones.label: Years of monitoring confirm lasting performance
milestones.explanation: Field monitoring over years would have to show that property loss and deformation stay within preset limits under realistic loads and exposure. This would establish durability over the observed period.

milestones.label: Independent sites meet preset cost limits
milestones.explanation: Independent trials across varied soils and groundwater conditions would have to meet preset affordability limits using full costs against equivalent alternatives. This would test repeatability and practical value.

uncertain: The relative capabilities and costs of bacterial treatment, conventional mixing, injected binders and other approaches remain unsettled.
Convincing acceptance limits, sampling coverage, monitoring duration and affordability thresholds still need definition.
Safe treatment beneath occupied districts and stabilization of thawing frozen ground need application-specific demonstrations.
